newsitem.title: USA: Helms sets conditions for action on chemical arms.
newsitem.headline: Helms sets conditions for action on chemical arms.

text.p: Conservative Sen. Jesse Helms set steep hurdles on Monday to U.S. Senate consideration of a global chemical weapons treaty.

Helms, chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, urged Republican Leader Trent Lott to focus on several other security-related issues before dealing with the treaty and called for a series of conditions to Senate approval.

The North Carolina Republican, long a foe of the 1993 Chemical Weapons Convention, said in a letter to Lott that "as it now stands (it) is fraught with deficiencies totally inimical to the national security interests of the United States."

The Clinton administration wants the Senate to approve the treaty before April 29 -- 60 days after its ratification by the 65th country. If the United States does not ratify the pact by that date it would have no say in administration of the ban.

As committee chairman, Helms has the power to prevent the treaty from going to the Senate floor. In a letter to Lott, he listed other Republican priorities that he said should come first, saying that when they had become law "we can turn our attention to the matter of the CWC."

On Helms's list were legislation to restructure U.S. "antiquated foreign policy agencies," reforming the United Nations, submitting modifications of two other weapons treaties to the Senate and enactment of legislation to deploy a national missile defence system.
Last year Helms had a months-long battle with the administration over his plan to reorganize the U.S. State Department. The plan was killed by a presidential veto.

Helms also proposed conditions on Senate approval of the treaty, barring formal U.S. ratification until Russia had committed to fulfil its pledges on destruction of chemical weapons and until the president certified that compliance by other signatories could be monitored with a high degree of confidence.
Helms also said the United States should not become a party to the treaty until other countries posing a threat to the United States had also joined.
Responding to Helms's conditions, White House spokesman David Johnson said: "We are working with the Senate on a bipartisan basis to take up the CWC on its merits."
A senior White House official said discussions with Senate leaders had been constructive.

The treaty was before the Senate last year but was withdrawn when it appeared the it would not receive the two-thirds majority required for approval during the heat of a presidential election campaign.
